citation: Al-Subaiey, A. et al. (2024). Novel interpretable and robust web-based AI platform for phishing email detection. arXiv:2405.11619.

modules.title: Data and Features
modules.question: What is in the dataset, and how does each email become a row of numbers?
modules.takeaway: 81,885 emails remain after removing 5 empty bodies and 596 duplicates. Phishing comes from only two corpora, so class and source overlap.

modules.title: Descriptive Statistics
modules.question: How do length, links, capitals and exclamation marks differ by class?
modules.takeaway: All four features are strongly right-skewed, so medians describe them better than means. Phishing emails are longer and use more capitals; spam is shortest.

modules.title: Random Variables and Bayes
modules.question: If a red flag fires, how likely is the email to be phishing?
modules.takeaway: Worked example at a 1% prior: P(phishing | has_credential) = (0.7420 x 0.0100) / (0.7420 x 0.0100 + 0.0731 x 0.9900) = 0.0074 / 0.0798 = 0.0930 The same evidence is far weaker when phishing is rare.

modules.title: Correlation and Regression
modules.question: Which features move with phishing, and can a straight line predict it?
modules.takeaway: The linear probability model explains R squared = 0.577, but 37.1% of its fitted probabilities fall outside [0, 1].

modules.title: Probability Distributions
modules.question: Which textbook distributions describe the data, and which fail?
modules.takeaway: The lognormal fits body length best in every class; link counts are far too dispersed for a Poisson; Nazario arrival gaps look exponential.

modules.title: Large-Sample Tests
modules.question: Are the differences between phishing and legitimate mail real, and how large are they?
modules.takeaway: With thousands of emails nearly every test rejects; effect sizes show which differences matter. A Type I error is a false alarm: declaring that a feature separates phishing from legitimate mail when it does not, held at alpha = 0.05. A Type II error is a missed phish: failing to detect a real difference, and power (1 - beta) is the chance of catching it.

modules.title: Small Samples, Chi-square and ANOVA
modules.question: What survives small samples, which features depend on class, and how do groups compare?
modules.takeaway: With about 57k emails almost any difference is significant; Cramer's V and the odds ratio show which ones matter. Observational data arranged in DOE layouts: classes were not randomly assigned, so effects are associations, not causal treatment effects. CRD = the one-way ANOVA above.

modules.title: Reliability
modules.question: If each red-flag rule is a component, how reliable is the system for one user?
modules.takeaway: At 1% phishing, a missed phish arrives about every 393 emails (7.9 days at 50 emails a day). Rules fire together, so independence overstates detection.

modules.title: PhishScore Validation
modules.question: How well does a transparent naive Bayes score do on unseen emails?
modules.takeaway: Sensitivity 0.746 and specificity 0.969, AUC 0.920. At 1% prevalence precision is only 0.196, and sensitivity drops by 0.413 on an unseen corpus.
